Option "Create two separate Dockerfiles…" is incorrect because Dockerfiles alone define the build process for images, but Elastic Beanstalk does not natively combine multiple standalone Dockerfiles in a multicontainer environment; instead, it expects a Dockerrun.aws.json v2 definition.

Option "Define the multi-container setup exclusively via .ebextensions…" is incorrect, since .ebextensions can be used for environment or instance configuration, but not for explicitly orchestrating and defining how multiple containers run together on Elastic Beanstalk.

Tip: When deploying multiple containers in Elastic Beanstalk, always use Dockerrun.aws.json v2, which is designed for multicontainer environments and integrates with ECS under the hood.

To successfully connect your on-premises Ubuntu 16.04 LTS servers to AWS CodeDeploy, several specific requirements must be met:

  • The user account managing the server setup must possess either sudo or root privileges. This is required because the CodeDeploy agent installation and certain operations need administrative rights to make changes to the system files and configurations.
  • The server should be registered with an IAM identity that has the required permissions for CodeDeploy registration. Proper IAM credentials (IAM user or role with CodeDeploy registration permissions) ensure secure communication and allow the server to interact with AWS CodeDeploy as needed.

The incorrect options are as follows:

  • Outbound connectivity to AWS service endpoints via port 80 must be permitted from the on-premises server. This is incorrect because CodeDeploy does not require outbound access over port 80; it generally communicates over port 443 (HTTPS) for secure communication with AWS endpoints.
  • It is necessary to set up either a VPN or AWS Direct Connect between the datacenter and AWS. While these options enhance security and reliability, they are not mandatory prerequisites. Public internet access to AWS endpoints is sufficient if security policies allow.
  • Java 8 installation is required for CodeDeploy agent functionality. This is a common misconception. The CodeDeploy agent is written in Ruby for Linux-based systems (like Ubuntu), so Java is not a necessity for the agent to run correctly.

Tip: Always ensure that the server has network access to AWS CodeDeploy endpoints (generally via HTTPS/port 443), and review the required permissions in the associated IAM entity for trouble-free registration and deployment.

By designating specific IAM users (in this case, senior developers) as 'approval pool members', only those users can satisfy approval requirements for merging pull requests. Associating the template with all repositories ensures compliance across the organization with minimal ongoing operational effort.

The best approach among these options is the secondary ELB with Route53 Weighted Round Robin traffic distribution. Using this setup, you can methodically control the percentage of users routed to the updated application stack with fine precision, down to one percent increments, thanks to the weighted records. Rollback is rapid and simple—just switch the DNS weights to direct traffic back to the original environment. This meets all the listed requirements: gradual rollout, precise user percentage control, and quick recovery.

'Use the Blue-Green deployment pattern' (Blue-Green) lets you cut over all users at once to new instances, but this approach cannot adjust traffic proportionally over time; it’s an all-or-nothing switchover, so it fails the requirement of granular traffic control.

'Replace your existing Launch Configuration’s AMI' (AMIs in Launch Config) and scaling old/new instances allows for gradual replacement but lacks the ability to precisely control what percentage of users see which version at a given time, given that ELB load balancing is instance-based, not user-percentage or version-based.

'Switch to AWS Elastic Beanstalk' provides convenient deployment mechanisms (like Rolling Deployments and rollbacks), but these don’t enable you to adjust user exposure to the new version at a granular, percentage-based level during a rollout.

Tip: To control user exposure down to the percentage level in AWS, leveraging multiple ELBs with Route53 weighted DNS records is a common and reliable solution.

The correct answers are: The main database instance is unintentionally deleted and There is a failure of RDS hardware on the primary instance.

A Read Replica keeps an asynchronous copy of the primary database. If the original database is lost—such as in the case where the main database instance is unintentionally deleted—or if there is a failure of RDS hardware on the primary instance, the Read Replica can be promoted to replace the source as it contains all data replicated up to the most recent point.

The other choices are not suitable recovery scenarios:

  • A bug in the application has accidentally erased some records from the primary database. – Deletions made at the source are also replicated to the replica, so deleted data cannot be recovered from the Read Replica.
  • The AWS account containing the databases has been compromised. – If the AWS account itself is compromised, all resources within that account are at risk, including the Read Replica, making it unavailable as a recovery option.
  • A regional outage impacts both ap-southeast-1 and ap-southeast-2 at the same time. – Since both the source and the replica are affected, it would not be possible to recover data from the Read Replica.

Tips: Use Read Replicas across regions for high availability and disaster recovery only if the disaster is localized to one region or the source instance itself. Remember, logical errors (such as unintentional deletions or bad application logic) are always replicated, so snapshots or backups are better suited to protect against such issues.

Intrinsic functions are permitted only in chosen sections such as in output values, within resource properties, in the metadata area, and for update policy attributes. This is because AWS CloudFormation restricts the use of intrinsic functions and does not support them for every field in a template. You should use intrinsic functions inside resource properties (for dynamically referencing values such as ARNs or resource names), outputs (to pass values to other stacks or display to users), metadata (for supplementing resource definitions), and update policy attributes (for controlling resource updates).

The option "Intrinsic functions can be placed throughout any portion of the template, with no restrictions." is incorrect, since sections like AWSTemplateFormatVersion and Description only accept literal values, and do not interpret intrinsic functions. Similarly, "It is possible to use intrinsic functions anywhere except inside the AWSTemplateFormatVersion and Description sections." is not accurate, because support is explicitly limited to certain template areas. "You may only insert intrinsic functions within the properties of resources." is also incorrect, as intrinsic functions are also allowed in outputs, metadata, and update policies in addition to resource properties.

The best solution is to use a mapping template on the Integration Request to filter out obsolete fields from the incoming JSON requests, ensuring that only valid fields are forwarded to the Lambda backend. This approach is correct because it mediates the request between the clients (who may still be sending old data) and the upgraded Lambda (which expects the new format), effectively allowing both old and new clients to coexist until migration is complete.

  • Set up a canary deployment stage in the original API to monitor ongoing use of the outdated JSON fields before deprecating the service.: This option does not solve the problem—it merely tracks usage and doesn't prevent outdated data from reaching the Lambda.
  • Apply a mapping template to the Integration Request to strip away deprecated fields from incoming JSON, ensuring only current values are sent to the Lambda function.: This is the correct approach because the Integration Request mapping template can modify the body of the requests before they reach the backend, allowing seamless filtering of legacy fields.
  • Integrate a new Lambda function as an authorizer in the original API so only well-formatted JSON requests are permitted to reach the backend.: Lambda authorizers are typically used for authentication and authorization, not for filtering request data or transforming payloads.
  • Configure a mapping template within the Integration Response to filter obsolete fields from the Lambda's output before returning a response to clients.: The Integration Response mapping only affects the response that goes back to the client after Lambda has already processed the request, so this does not help filter fields out before reaching Lambda.

Tips: Use Integration Request mapping templates to modify inputs to Lambda, and Integration Response mapping templates to alter outputs to the client. Always transform data as close to the source as possible to ensure backend compatibility.

The correct answer is Amazon S3, as it offers limitless storage capacity, scales automatically, and is both highly available and very durable.

Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is designed to provide industry-leading scalability, data availability, security, and performance. It removes the need for you to predict storage requirements up-front, as storage automatically expands to handle any amount of data with no manual intervention. This fits perfectly for startups with little capital and ever-growing data needs.

Let's break down why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Amazon Import/Export, since it helps migrate large quantities of data directly into Amazon S3: This service is useful for transferring large volumes of data into AWS, but it is not itself a storage solution. It’s typically used once at the beginning or when transferring huge datasets offline, but you still need S3 or another destination for storage.
  • Amazon EC2, given that EBS volumes can scale to any required amount when paired with Auto Scaling, thus providing high availability and fault tolerance: EC2 and EBS volumes are best for block storage attached to compute instances. Although you can add and scale EBS volumes, there is a maximum size for EBS volumes, and they do not offer the same virtually unlimited storage and seamless scaling as S3.
  • Amazon Glacier, to minimize storage expenses while scaling to accommodate limitless data amounts: While Amazon Glacier (now known as Amazon S3 Glacier) is extremely cost-effective for long-term archival, it is intended for infrequently accessed data and has high retrieval latency. It's not suitable for active or real-time data storage needs.

Tip: When you need a solution that provides unbounded, scalable storage with minimal administrative overhead, Amazon S3 should be your go-to choice. Always remember to match your storage service to your usage patterns and access requirements!

The correct approach is to update the launch configuration to use C3 in your CloudFormation template and add an UpdatePolicy for AutoScalingRollingUpdate, then run a stack update. The UpdatePolicy ensures rolling updates, which means old instances are gradually replaced with new ones running the C3 instance type, minimizing downtime for users.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Make changes to the AWS Management Console, creating a new launch configuration for C3 instances, then update the Auto Scaling group with this configuration. Existing instances will automatically switch instance types. – This is incorrect because existing instances do not change their type automatically (live in-place modification is not possible); they are only replaced as part of scaling actions or rolling updates.
  • Directly update the existing launch configuration through the AWS Management Console to use C3 instances, and add an UpdatePolicy of AutoScalingRollingUpdate to your Auto Scaling group. – This option suggests editing an existing launch configuration, but launch configurations are immutable; you must create a new one. Also, changes through the console don’t link to CloudFormation management and can cause drift from the stack.
  • Change the launch configuration to use C3 in your CloudFormation template, then update the stack with this template. Automatic replacement of the instances with new types will follow. – While this updates the launch configuration, it does not specify an UpdatePolicy, so CloudFormation terminates and replaces all instances at once, causing disruption.

Tip: Always include an AutoScalingRollingUpdate UpdatePolicy for controlled Auto Scaling group updates using CloudFormation to ensure minimal service impact and smooth instance type transitions.

VPC Flow Logs primarily provide detailed information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces within your VPC. The following options are most accurate:

  • Details about TCP and UDP network traffic both accepted and rejected by your VPC, such as source/destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols.
    VPC Flow Logs capture this network traffic metadata, allowing you to analyze network behavior, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and support compliance efforts.
  • Records of network flow activity, including information about the allowed or denied traffic traversing network interfaces in your VPC.
    These logs document data like the source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, and the result (ACCEPT/REJECT), which is essential for monitoring and auditing your AWS environment.

The following options do not describe information available from VPC Flow Logs:

  • The daily peak traffic period affecting your EC2-hosted web application. – While you could infer some traffic patterns from Flow Logs, these logs do not specifically highlight application load peaks or traditional web analytics.
  • The total number of objects transferred to S3 buckets under your AWS accounts. – Flow Logs track network connections, not object storage activity metrics in S3.
  • The moment when SQS queue messages hit their capacity limit. – SQS metrics are monitored separately via CloudWatch, not VPC Flow Logs, which focus on network traffic.
  • The occurrence of customized CloudWatch alarms triggered on EC2 instances. – Alarms and their events are managed through CloudWatch, not captured in VPC Flow Logs.
  • The AWS Region with the greatest number of application users. – VPC Flow Logs don't provide user distribution statistics or geographic analytics.

Tip: Always remember that VPC Flow Logs focus strictly on tracking the network-level details for security, auditing, and troubleshooting—not application or service-level events.

  • MFA Delete & Versioning: Enabling versioning ensures object integrity by preserving every version of S3 objects. Requiring MFA for deletions protects against accidental or malicious data loss because even users with high privileges must provide an MFA code to delete contents. This combination is a best practice for safeguarding critical data integrity in S3.
  • IAM Role for EC2: Assigning an IAM role to EC2 instances for S3 access is the recommended, secure way to allow applications to interact with S3 without managing or exposing long-lived credentials. This reduces the risk of credential leakage, simplifies permission management, and helps enforce least privilege.

Incorrect answers:

  • "Deploy a configuration management tool to distribute IAM user credentials to your EC2 servers. Use these credentials to pull code updates from S3 securely."—Avoid distributing permanent IAM credentials; IAM roles are more secure and scalable.
  • "Write an S3 bucket policy to allow access solely from EC2 private (RFC 1918) IPs, and turn on versioning."—While limiting by IP can improve security, Amazon EC2's public IPs might change and restricting by private RFC 1918 ranges does not guarantee security or that only your EC2 instances can access the bucket.
  • "Set up AWS Data Pipeline to move bucket content into Amazon Glacier weekly for lifecycle management."—Lifecycle policies are used for archiving, not for code deployment or integrity management.
  • "Utilize AWS Data Pipeline, integrating MFA, to push code securely from S3 to your EC2 instances."—MFA is not integrated into AWS Data Pipeline operations, and Data Pipeline is not appropriate for secure code deployments from S3 to EC2.

Tip: Use S3 versioning and MFA delete for robust object-level data protection, and always choose IAM roles over user credential distribution on EC2.

The correct answer is EC2Instance: Type: "AWS::EC2::Instance" Properties: InstanceType: !If [CreateProdResources, c1.xlarge, m1.large]. If the condition is true (production), the value c1.xlarge is used for the InstanceType; otherwise (development), it uses m1.large.

  • EC2Instance: Type: "AWS::EC2::Instance" Properties: InstanceType: Fn::Not: [CreateProdResources, m1.large, c1.xlarge] — Fn::Not does not select between values; it returns true or false. It's incorrect for dynamically setting InstanceType.

Tip: Use !If when you need to conditionally assign property values; use the top-level Condition only to control resource creation. Review CloudFormation intrinsic functions to understand these differences!

The CloudWatch Logs Agent can stream log data directly from your instance to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, allowing centralized log collection even if instances are terminated unexpectedly or due to scaling events.

The options Modify Auto Scaling group policies to perform backups of ephemeral storage when instances terminate and Set Auto Scaling policies to create a snapshot of all temporary instance storage upon termination are incorrect because ephemeral storage is local instance storage that cannot be backed up or snapshotted when the instance is terminated; all data on ephemeral storage is lost upon shutdown or termination.

The choice Install and configure the CloudWatch monitoring agent on your AMI, and use an SNS alert based on CloudWatch metrics to trigger log backups from the ephemeral drive is not appropriate because the monitoring agent does not provide a native feature to do file-level log backups. Relying on metrics and alerts to backup logs from ephemeral storage is a complex workaround and not supported out-of-the-box.

Tip: For applications running on ephemeral storage, always utilize an agent (like CloudWatch Logs Agent or a similar solution) to forward logs in real-time to persistent and centralized log storage to avoid data loss during instance scale-in events.

This condition is NOT required for forwarding CloudWatch Events to a master account's event bus. This means accounts can be standalone or part of multiple organizations—they do not have to share a single AWS Organization for cross-account event delivery to work.

  • The main (master) account must allow the receipt of CloudWatch events from other AWS accounts.: This is essential. Without proper permissions and policy configuration, the master account's event bus will not accept incoming events from other accounts.

  • The sender accounts require an appropriate IAM role to forward events to the master account's event bus.: This is necessary for secure cross-account operations, ensuring only authorized accounts can send events.
  • The event's target in CloudWatch Events should be set to 'Event bus in another AWS account' for transmission to the master account.: Without specifying the correct target, the event will not reach the intended event bus in the master account.

Tip: Remember, AWS Organizations simplifies management of multiple accounts but is not required for basic cross-account integrations like EventBridge event forwarding. Always ensure correct permissions and targets are configured for successful cross-account communication.

The best solution is to deploy two instances of your stateless API in different AWS regions and configure Route53 Latency Based Routing with failover to direct traffic to the optimal region. This method leverages Route53's health checks and failover so clients are automatically routed to the healthy, low-latency region. Using Auto Scaling Groups behind ELBs in both regions guarantees your deployment is elastic and resilient, even during a regional AWS failure.

The other options are not sufficient for regional failures:

  • Set up a CloudFront distribution in front of your API. Even if your region encounters downtime, CloudFront's edge infrastructure ensures service continuity. – CloudFront can cache static data and mitigate certain disruptions, but if the API's origin is entirely unavailable due to a regional outage, CloudFront cannot serve dynamic API responses that require a live backend.
  • Utilize an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) with cross-zone load balancing for redundancy across data centers, guaranteeing availability if one availability zone is lost. – Cross-zone load balancing helps within a single region but won't protect against complete regional failures, as the ELB itself operates only inside its home region.
  • Create a Route53 Weighted Round Robin DNS record, so if one region goes down, that region can redirect users to another operational region. – Weighted routing doesn't provide health checks or automated failover, and if a region goes down, that weighted endpoint won’t be able to perform redirects or respond, resulting in downtime for users routed to the failed region.

Key tip: Stateless APIs are easier to deploy across multiple regions for disaster recovery. By pairing multi-region deployments with Route53's advanced routing and health checks, you achieve high resiliency to regional outages.

The Weighted policy for both Blue/Green and Canary deployments, and Failover policy for Disaster Recovery is the best match for the routing needs described.

  • Blue/Green deployment typically requires managing how much traffic is directed to the old (Blue) and new (Green) environments. The weighted routing policy allows you to smoothly shift traffic between two different resource sets by adjusting weights.
  • Canary deployment benefits from the Weighted policy as well, since you can direct a small percentage of user requests to the new version before gradually increasing the traffic—ensuring smooth rollouts with less risk.
  • Disaster Recovery is best handled with the Failover policy, which routes traffic to a primary resource, but automatically shifts to a backup destination if the primary becomes unhealthy, supporting robust DR strategies.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Weighted policy for Blue/Green deployment, Latency policy for Canary deployment, and Failover policy for Disaster Recovery: Latency-based routing is not suitable for Canary deployments, as it doesn’t provide granular control of traffic percentages.
  • Simple policy for Blue/Green deployment, Weighted policy for Canary deployment, and Latency policy for Disaster Recovery: Simple routing cannot help with traffic shifting needed for Blue/Green, and Latency policy is not for DR situations.
  • Latency policy for Blue/Green deployment, Simple policy for Canary deployment, and Weighted policy for Disaster Recovery: Latency and simple policies do not give the control necessary for deployment strategies, and weighted routing is not for disaster recovery scenarios; failover is the better choice.

Tip: Use Weighted policies for progressive rollouts and deployments (Blue/Green, Canary), and Failover for high availability and DR setups in Route 53.

The best choice is DynamoDB table where read throughput significantly surpasses write throughput by 100x, with CloudFront used for caching. Here’s why:

  • Your workload is predominantly read-heavy (100:1 ratio). Thus, provisioning a table to specifically handle much higher read operations optimizes both performance and cost.
  • CloudFront is well-suited for caching highly popular items worldwide, especially the top 1% of frequently accessed scores, reducing DynamoDB’s read load further and distributing content with low latency.

The other options don't align as well for these reasons:

  • DynamoDB provisioned to handle 100 times more reads than writes, using ElastiCache for caching results. While ElastiCache is great for low-latency in-memory caching, it is typically best fit for complex query or stateful application caches rather than large-scale read optimization for global, uniformly accessed APIs. CloudFront offers global edge caching that can better target the top 1% of popular data.
  • DynamoDB with balanced read and write capacity, leveraging CloudFront for caching hot data. Using equal read and write capacity provisioning under-provisions the read side and may result in throttling, given the 100:1 access ratio.
  • DynamoDB table with comparable read and write capacity, integrated with DAX caching. DAX is a DynamoDB-specific in-memory cache and does help with read-heavy workloads, but paired with equal read/write throughput, it isn’t tailored to your needs and would not fully take advantage of the API’s read-heavy traffic patterns.

Tip: Always align provisioned capacity with real-world request patterns. For read-heavy systems, ensure read capacity is prioritized, and use caching with a worldwide distribution where hot data is intensely accessed. CloudFront excels at caching frequently requested content, especially for API endpoints fetching high-score data.

The best ways to safeguard data on an EBS volume are:

Copy the current, unencrypted snapshot and select the option to encrypt the replica. All volumes made from this encrypted snapshot will also be encrypted. This method allows you to generate an encrypted volume from your existing unencrypted data by first creating a snapshot, then copying it while enabling encryption. When you restore an EBS volume from this encrypted snapshot, it will be fully encrypted, providing an effective way to secure previously unencrypted EBS data.

Provision a new, encrypted EBS volume, attach it, migrate your data onto it, and remove the unencrypted EBS volume. This approach entails creating a new encrypted volume and moving all sensitive files to it. Once you verify data integrity on the encrypted volume, you can delete the original unencrypted volume. Both practices comply with AWS security standards for at-rest encryption.

Detach the EBS volume, create a snapshot, and enable encryption on the snapshot. Then reattach the EBS volume. is incorrect because you cannot directly enable encryption on an existing snapshot. The proper approach is to copy the snapshot and enable encryption during the copy operation.

  • { "source": [ "aws.codedeploy" ], "detail-type": [ "CodeDeploy Instance State-change Notification" ], "detail": { "state": [ "FAILURE", "SUCCESS", "READY", "START" ] } }: This pattern matches individual instance changes within a deployment, producing excessive noise and not indicating full deployment outcomes.

  • { "source": [ "aws.codedeploy" ], "detail-type": [ "CodeDeploy Instance State-change Notification" ], "detail": { "state": [ "FAILURE", "START" ] } }: This option also focuses on instance-level changes and misses the SUCCESS state that is critical for deployment completions. It will not capture all necessary deployment outcomes.

When configuring event patterns for deployment notifications, always use detail-type CodeDeploy Deployment State-change Notification and select only the states relevant for full deployments (typically FAILURE and SUCCESS). To secure data at rest and in transit on AWS, the following methods are recommended:

  • Enable encryption for all EBS disks attached to EC2 Virtual Machines. Encrypting EBS volumes ensures that data stored on these disks is protected at rest. This is a best practice to defend against unauthorized access, especially if the volumes or snapshots are compromised.
  • Apply server-side encryption measures for S3 buckets. This protects your data stored in S3 by automatically encrypting it before writing it to disk and decrypting it when accessed, ensuring confidentiality for data at rest.
  • Utilize SSL/HTTPS protocols with Elastic Load Balancers. By using SSL/TLS with your ELB, data transmitted between clients and the load balancer (and often between the load balancer and backend) is secured while in transit, guarding against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks.

The incorrect option, Leverage IOPS-based EBS volumes when launching EC2 Instances, does not provide additional security for data at rest or in transit. Instead, using IOPS volumes (provisioned IOPS SSD) is related to optimizing performance and IO throughput, not data security. Always focus on encryption mechanisms (for data at rest) and secured transport protocols (for data in transit) to maximize security.

The optimal filter pattern is Pattern: [ip, user, username, timestamp, request, status_code matching 4**, bytes]. This pattern makes use of the 4** wildcard to match all log lines where the status code falls within the 4xx range (such as 404, 403, 400, etc.) and includes the key 'bytes' to capture the relevant field. This approach ensures precise detection of all client error responses irrespective of the specific 4xx code.

Examining the other options:

  • Pattern: [..., 4xx status code, bytes]: While this option attempts to match 4xx status codes, the syntax is ambiguous and would not be recognized properly by CloudWatch metric filters.
  • Pattern: [ip, user, username, timestamp, request, status_code is like 4xx, bytes]: This pattern uses non-standard phrasing ('is like'), which CloudWatch metric filters do not support, and could result in no log lines matching.
  • Pattern: [..., status_code equals 4*, bytes]: The use of 'equals 4*' is incorrect pattern matching for CloudWatch, where '**' should be used as the wildcard for any digits, not '*'.

Tip: In CloudWatch metric filter patterns, use '**' to match patterns such as an entire range of HTTP status codes (4xx or 5xx) across log events. Always ensure your filter pattern mirrors both the structure and the order of log fields in your source logs.

The main challenge with weighted routing policies in Route53 is the impact of DNS Time To Live (TTL). When you update the DNS records to shift traffic between blue and green environments, the TTL setting determines how long clients cache the DNS response. This means that, even after you direct all new traffic to the green environment, some users may continue to connect to the blue environment if their DNS cache hasn't expired. This could slow down both the rollout of new environments and any potential rollback since old DNS responses may still point to the previous environment.

The correct response is: The effectiveness of the transition to a new environment may be hindered by DNS TTL since clients can cache DNS responses, potentially extending connectivity to the previous environment beyond the intended switch.

'Using a weighted routing policy in Route53 is inherently too complex to operate within a CICD deployment pipeline': This is inaccurate; weighted routing is straightforward to incorporate in automation and pipelines.

'A routing policy that is weighted within Route53 is never appropriate in situations where a rollback is needed.': This is not entirely correct; rollback is possible, though DNS caching can make the process slower.

'Only Classic Load Balancers are supported for this approach; Application and Network Load Balancers cannot be paired with weighted routing in Route53.': Both Application and Network Load Balancers are supported with Route53 weighted routing.

Tip: To mitigate TTL issues, use shorter DNS TTL values when deploying blue/green strategies with DNS-based routing.

Let's review why the other options are incorrect:

  • "Scale horizontally by deploying multiple independent DynamoDB tables." — DynamoDB tables can't simply be deployed in parallel this way for load distribution without complex changes to your data model and application logic, and this isn't a recommended scaling approach.

  • "Simply increase the write capacity units for your DynamoDB table whenever high load is expected." — Although raising capacity can handle more writes, this is a reactive approach and might not be cost-efficient or quick enough during sudden spikes. It's also harder to predict peak loads precisely, and alone doesn't buffer or smooth request bursts.

Tips: Integrate SQS (or similar message queues) to absorb sudden request bursts and allow DynamoDB to keep up with a steady rate of writes. Also consider using DynamoDB Auto Scaling for dynamically adjusting throughput.

The correct answer is to assign an IAM role to your Amazon EC2 instance and use that IAM role to access the Amazon RDS database. This approach leverages AWS best practices for security by eliminating the need to store static credentials on the instances and instead using temporary credentials automatically provided by the IAM role. This reduces the risk of credential leakage and is the recommended method for secure access management.

Let's review the other options:

  • "Launch an EC2 instance, use your configuration management tool to inject Amazon RDS database credentials into the instance, and then create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) out of this configured EC2." This approach is insecure because the credentials become part of the AMI and thus are potentially accessible to anyone launching instances from that AMI.
  • "Add the Amazon RDS database credentials to the EC2 instance's user data and retrieve them on instance boot." Storing sensitive credentials in user data is not recommended, since user data can be retrieved from within the instance even after startup and can lead to unintentional exposure.
  • "Grant EC2 instances an IAM role allowing them to read from a private Amazon S3 bucket where a file with RDS credentials is stored, and use your configuration management tool to fetch this file as needed." Although this method leverages IAM roles and S3 permissions, it still requires managing static credentials within S3, and those credentials could be exposed if not managed carefully. It is better to avoid storing static database credentials and use IAM roles directly when possible.

Tip: Using IAM roles is the safest and most scalable way to provide temporary and automatically-rotated credentials to AWS resources, maintaining principle of least privilege and reducing credential management overhead.

The correct approach is to develop a fresh launch configuration with the new AMI and associate it to the Auto Scaling group. Temporarily increase the group's capacity to six, and once the new instances are running and operational, scale back down to three. This staged rollout, known as a blue/green or rolling deployment, ensures uninterrupted application availability while new instances are launched. Once the replacement instances have passed all health and application checks, the desired capacity can be reduced, and older instances will be terminated automatically by the Auto Scaling group. This prevents service disruption if any of the new instances are slow to start or fail initial health or application checks.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Update the launch configuration itself instead of altering the Auto Scaling group settings: Merely updating the launch configuration or the Auto Scaling group alone does not replace existing running instances. Old EC2s will still serve traffic until they're manually replaced, so this approach does not assure a proper deployment.
  • Manually terminate the existing instances that use the previous launch configuration: This process can disrupt availability and may cause downtime if the replacement instances take longer to initialize or fail to launch correctly. An orchestrated, rolling approach avoids this risk.
  • Provision a new ELB and attach the existing Auto Scaling group to it: This does not address the core deployment sequencing issue. Creating a new ELB without changing the rollout procedure does not resolve the errors experienced during deployment.

Tip: Always ensure your deployment process allows enough time for new instances to fully initialize and pass not just health checks, but application-level readiness, before decommissioning old ones.

This workflow is not suitable for hourly reporting needs.

The best step is to configure the health check of the Classic ELB to point to the application or a webpage that clearly reflects when Tomcat is fully initialized and ready to serve traffic. Often, Classic ELB's default HTTP health check only validates whether the HTTP port responds, not whether the actual application on the instance is ready. With Tomcat (or other Java applications), it can take several seconds or minutes for the application server to fully start and deploy all web apps. If the ELB health check points to a simple endpoint that returns a success response before Tomcat (and your app) is fully ready, traffic will be sent too soon, causing Tomcat errors until initialization completes.

Why the other options are not recommended:
"Extend the waiting period" doesn't guarantee the application is ready, as initialization time can vary -- using an accurate health check is more reliable.
"Deploy Application Load Balancer with HTTPS health checks" is not required; Classic ELB supports URL health checks as well. Switching load balancers adds unnecessary complexity for this problem.
"Switch to Application Load Balancer since only it can truly confirm status" is incorrect. Classic ELB can point health checks to any application-specific URL. The key is to ensure that the health check endpoint returns success only when all components (including Tomcat and the application) are ready, regardless of the load balancer type.

Tip: Design your health check endpoint in Tomcat to return a healthy response only after all dependencies are loaded and the app is operational. This prevents premature routing of traffic and the associated errors.

The most effective way to diagnose slow response times for an application behind an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) is to review the Elastic Load Balancer access logs. These logs provide detailed information about request processing times, backend latency, client and target IPs, response codes, and more. By investigating these logs, you can pinpoint whether delays are from the load balancer's processing or the backend servers themselves, and identify patterns correlated with the new feature.

The option to log all API activities with CloudTrail and comb through the logs to discover clues is not directly helpful for performance issues since CloudTrail is better for tracking AWS API calls for security, auditing, and compliance rather than pinpointing response delays for web requests.

While track CPU usage over time with CloudWatch to spot any CPU spikes correlating with issues might help detect if there are resource bottlenecks, it does not necessarily point to whether the source of latency lies at the ELB or another part of your app—plus, not all performance problems are caused by CPU exhaustion.

Setting up custom CloudWatch metrics tailored to critical application features can provide insight for future incidents, but won't immediately help you diagnose the current problem unless those metrics were already in place before the issue began.

Tip: Always enable ELB access logs in production environments as a best practice to help with swift diagnostics when problems arise.

The correct answer is Identify the compute bottleneck, use that as the scaling metric, and set CloudWatch alarm thresholds to values that trigger scaling only when performance starts to degrade. This approach ensures that scaling actions are based on the specific metric that accurately reflects system performance bottlenecks rather than arbitrary metrics such as CPU utilization alone, which may not fully capture the workload nature. Setting thresholds aligned to when user-facing latency or performance issues first arise provides responsive yet stable scaling behavior.

Here's why the other options are less effective:

  • Increase the Auto Scaling cooldown period to ensure additional instances have more startup time before new scaling actions occur. — While cooldowns prevent repeated scale-outs before new instances are ready, they don’t directly address the root problem: scaling decisions based on inappropriate or overly sensitive metrics, which still causes over-provisioning or sluggish scale-down.
  • Switch to larger EC2 instance types so fewer are needed and the Auto Scaling Group doesn't scale out as frequently. — This can sometimes reduce the total number of instances, but the fundamental issue is still there if scaling is triggered for the wrong reasons; you might just have more powerful idle resources wasting cost.
  • Raise the CloudWatch alarm thresholds on your auto scaling group to require much higher demand before scaling up. — Raising thresholds only delays scaling action, which could lead to slow responses during actual spikes, and only masks rather than solves the underlying metric-related problems.

Tip: Choosing metrics like application response time, request queue length, or specific resource limitations helps ensure the Auto Scaling Group reacts proportionally to real load, reducing the risk of unnecessary over-scaling and cost.

The correct answer is: Associate distinct tags to your test and production EC2 instances, and implement IAM policy conditions that grant permissions only for instances with authorized tags.

This solution leverages resource-level permissions in AWS. By tagging EC2 instances (for example, with Environment: Production or Environment: Development), you can write IAM policies that use these tags as conditions, restricting users or groups to only operate on resources with matching tags. This ensures proper segmentation and least privilege, and is highly scalable and flexible for permissions management.

  • Deploy your test and production instances in separate VPCs, and connect them with VPC peering. – This option separates network boundaries but does not address IAM permission boundaries. VPC peering is for connectivity, not fine-grained access control. It doesn't prevent a user with sufficient IAM rights from accessing instances in either environment.

In AWS, the common and scalable way to differentiate is by using resource tags.
  • Launch test and production instances in separate Availability Zones and enforce Multi-Factor Authentication for access. – Separating by Availability Zones does not isolate access at the instance or user level. MFA improves authentication security but does not help with segmentation between production and test resources.

Exam Tips: Always use tagging and IAM policy conditions for fine-grained access control on AWS resources. This is a core security best practice and strongly favored in the exam when segmentation is required.

Correct Answers:

- For the database tier, implement an Auto Scaling group and use the Amazon RDS read replica lag CloudWatch metric to automatically scale out read replicas.

Explanation:

  • The use of EC2 Auto Scaling (second option) makes the web server layer self-healing by automatically launching new instances if the current ones fail or are terminated. By tracking EC2's CPU utilization with CloudWatch, you can maintain enough capacity to handle varying load and replace unhealthy instances, making fault recovery automated.
  • Auto Scaling the read replicas in the database layer (fourth option) based on RDS read replica lag ensures that additional replicas are spun up as needed to handle increased read requests or failures, allowing the system to recover seamlessly if a read replica becomes unhealthy or lags behind.

Incorrect Options:

  • Create an Auto Scaling group for the web server tier and configure scaling based on Amazon RDS DB CPU utilization metrics provided by CloudWatch: This is incorrect because scaling the web tier should not be tied to the database's CPU utilization; scaling decisions for web servers should reflect their own workload metrics.
  • Resize both the EC2 instances for web servers and RDS database instances to larger instance types to prevent them from turning unhealthy: Simply using bigger instances doesn't make the system self-healing. It only increases resource allocation and doesn't address automatic recovery or failover.
  • Configure the database with an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ setup: While Multi-AZ allows automated failover for increased availability, it does not provide self-healing with regards to read scaling or replacing failed web/application servers. Multi-AZ applies to high availability of the primary database instance.

Tip: For architecting self-healing systems, focus on automated replacement/recovery (e.g., Auto Scaling groups, health checks, read replica scaling) rather than simply adding resources or availability features without automation.

AWS Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid cloud storage and backup, not for providing fast application and data restoration as needed here.

The best solution is to add a Global Secondary Index (GSI) where CityId is the partition key and HighestTemperature is the sort key. GSIs provide the flexibility to query data with entirely new key structures, independent of the table’s primary key. This allows your queries to efficiently fetch all temperature records for a city, sorted or filtered by their recorded highest temperature without restructuring the base table or migrating data.

Here’s why the other options are not correct:

  • Revise the current table to have CityId as the partition key and HighestTemperature as the sort key. — Modifying the primary key for an existing DynamoDB table is not feasible; you’d have to destroy and recreate the table, resulting in downtime and potential data loss.
  • Introduce a Local Secondary Index using CityId for the partition key and HighestTemperature for the sort key. — Local Secondary Indexes (LSIs) require the same partition key as the base table, which in this case is CountryId. Since CityId is different, an LSI cannot be used here.
  • Create both a Global Secondary Index with CityId as the partition key, and a separate Global Secondary Index with HighestTemperature as the partition key. This is required because the primary index only employs a single-partition key, so secondary indexes are restricted to single-partition keys as well. — This suggestion is not only inaccurate but also inefficient. GSIs can have both a partition key and a sort key. Furthermore, you only need one suitable GSI to cover your query requirement. The statement about GSIs being limited to a single attribute as a partition key is incorrect.

Tip: Use Global Secondary Indexes to support new and diverse query patterns in DynamoDB, particularly when querying relationships and attributes not included in the table’s primary key.

  • Deploy the application with AWS OpsWorks Stacks, set up a secondary stack, and reroute users via Route 53 when launching the updated application is not a typical Blue Green deployment strategy in AWS, and OpsWorks is less suited for web application deployment compared to Elastic Beanstalk.

Tip: For Blue Green on AWS, Elastic Beanstalk simplifies the process considerably and offers built-in features to manage deployment switching.

  • Read Replicas for RDS: Introducing Read Replicas to your RDS configuration improves database scalability by distributing the read workload.   • Enable an Auto Scaling Group for your RDS database servers, scaling them depending on utilization metrics tracked in CloudWatch.: RDS instances cannot be managed through Auto Scaling Groups. Scaling for RDS is handled differently (e.g., instance size changes, Read Replicas, and Multi-AZ), so this option isn't technically feasible.

Tips: Always pair Auto Scaling Groups with CloudWatch metrics for stateless, horizontally scalable application layers. For RDS, only use Read Replicas for scaling out reads, not writes, and remember that Multi-AZ is for availability, not direct scale or cost optimization.

The correct way to move your instance from Wait to InService after your health check passes is by using the complete-lifecycle-action AWS CLI command (or its API equivalent). When you configure an Auto Scaling group with a lifecycle hook, it pauses instances at 'Pending:Wait' or 'Terminating:Wait' until you signal that your custom actions are done. complete-lifecycle-action is designed to let Auto Scaling know when you are finished, so it can resume normal processing.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Run 'record-lifecycle-action-heartbeat'... - This action merely extends the timeout of the lifecycle hook but does not complete the process or transition the instance out of the Wait state.
  • Employ the 'attach-instances'... - This command is for attaching standalone EC2 instances to an Auto Scaling group. It doesn't signal lifecycle hook completion and will not move the instance from Wait to InService in this context.
  • Use the 'put-lifecycle-hook'... - This command creates or updates lifecycle hooks; it does not manage the completion or continuation of an individual instance through the hook.

Tip: Always use complete-lifecycle-action in your automation to exit custom Wait states and resume Auto Scaling's operations. Remember: heartbeat commands buy you more time, but complete-lifecycle-action is the signal that you're done!

The correct answers are Pending:Wait and Terminating:Wait. These two states correspond to scaling out and scaling in, respectively. When a lifecycle hook is added, instances entering the Pending state (being launched) move to Pending:Wait before becoming active, allowing additional setup or configuration tasks. Likewise, instances being terminated enter Terminating:Wait, pausing termination for extra actions like log collection or graceful shutdown.

Exiting:Wait and Launching:Wait are incorrect, as there are no such wait states in the Auto Scaling lifecycle. It's crucial to remember that only Pending:Wait (for launches) and Terminating:Wait (for terminations) are controllable through lifecycle hooks.

Tip: Associate Pending:Wait with scale-out/setup, and Terminating:Wait with scale-in/cleanup, so you can easily recall which hooks apply to which process.

When an instance in an Auto Scaling Group transitions to the Terminating:Wait state because of a lifecycle hook, you want to be automatically notified so you can investigate. The suitable AWS services for this notification are AWS SNS (Simple Notification Service) and Amazon CloudWatch Events (now part of EventBridge):

  • AWS SNS is a fully managed publish/subscribe messaging service that allows you to set up notifications triggered by Auto Scaling lifecycle events. You can directly connect lifecycle hooks to SNS topics to broadcast notifications.
  • Amazon CloudWatch Events can respond to state changes within AWS resources. You can configure a CloudWatch Event rule for the Auto Scaling event and target an SNS topic or Lambda function, ensuring real-time awareness of the lifecycle change.

Why other options are not suitable:

  • AWS CloudTrail records API activity for audit and compliance but does not have the same real-time alerting mechanisms for state transitions like lifecycle hooks.
  • AWS Config tracks configuration changes of AWS resources and compliance but does not natively trigger notifications for ASG instance lifecycle changes.
  • AWS Step Functions orchestrates workflows across services but isn't directly used for lifecycle or notification of ASG events.

Tip: Lifecycle hooks integrate easily with both CloudWatch Events and SNS, providing flexibility in how you handle notifications and interventions during instance state transitions.

By implementing its advice, you can remove over-provisioned resources, paying only for what you need, without risking performance or availability.

Additionally, shutting down non-production EC2 instances on weekends or after work hours is a highly practical method to avoid unnecessary spend. Many development or testing workloads don’t require 24/7 availability—turning these resources off can significantly reduce costs with zero impact on end-user service.

The other options are less suitable for the following reasons:

Switching from On-Demand to Spot Instances for Jenkins managing production CI/CD pipelines is risky, because Spot Instances can be interrupted with little notice, risking failed builds or deploys at critical moments—this can directly impact business operations.

Using Direct Connect instead of VPN does provide higher reliability and performance, but it is generally a more expensive solution rather than a cheaper one, especially for smaller workloads or companies without a consistent large data transfer need.

Choosing gp2 SSDs over Throughput Optimized HDDs (st1) in non-production environments is misguided since storage selection should align with workload needs: st1 volumes are often cheaper but are designed for high-throughput requirements, while gp2 volumes are optimized for IOPS. Blindly switching without workload analysis can actually increase costs or degrade performance.

Tip: Focus on matching resource type and size to workload, use automation to control resource schedules, and always verify that cost-saving actions don't jeopardize business-critical workloads.

Tip: Always assign permissions following the least privilege principle and avoid giving excessive access. For auditors, a custom policy with read-only rights to just the needed AWS resources is ideal.

The most effective way to achieve microsecond-level read latency in DynamoDB without changing existing application logic is to integrate DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX). DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB that significantly improves read times by reducing response latency from milliseconds to microseconds.

Let's review each option:

Enable on-demand capacity mode for your DynamoDB table. This setting allows DynamoDB to scale automatically according to usage patterns, but it does not decrease read latency into the microsecond range. Response times are still typically measured in milliseconds.

Add a Global Secondary Index to make querying the DynamoDB table more performant. While Global Secondary Indexes enhance query flexibility and can improve some read operations, they do not inherently reduce latency to the microsecond level. Performance improvements are only realized for the queries using those indexes.

Set up a read replica in another AWS Region by making the DynamoDB table Global. Global Tables are designed for high availability and providing local reads in multiple regions, but they do not offer microsecond latency, nor are they primarily intended to improve read speed within a single region.

In contrast, Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster to leverage faster, in-memory reads directly addresses performance by providing a managed cache that does not require application code changes, delivering the lowest possible read latency for DynamoDB workloads.

Tip: For applications where microsecond response for reads is a requirement, always consider AWS DAX before re-architecting your application or moving to alternative data stores.

Tip: Always monitor first, then deploy, validate with pre-traffic/post-traffic hooks, and shift traffic last to reduce user impact.

The Immutable deployment strategy in Elastic Beanstalk is specifically designed to ensure smooth upgrades and fast rollbacks without causing downtime or running two entire environments. With immutable deployments, Elastic Beanstalk provisions a new set of instances with the updated application version. These new instances must pass health checks before traffic is routed to them. If the new deployment is unhealthy, it can easily be terminated, reverting back to the original group of instances.

The other options are not optimal for this scenario:

  • Choose a Rolling with additional batch deployment strategy to launch extra instances for each update. – While this method does add extra instances temporarily and reduces downtime, it can still serve partial traffic to older or unhealthy versions during deployment, which does not fully mitigate risk of user disruption.
  • Implement a Rolling deployment by launching new app versions on new EC2 instances and then connecting them to the existing load balancer. – Regular Rolling updates replace instances in batches, which can lead to periods where some users are routed to the new, untested version before health checks complete. Problems with the new version could affect some users during deployment.
  • Utilize a Blue/Green deployment by swapping Elastic Beanstalk environment URLs. – This option does offer reliable rollbacks and no downtime, but it requires maintaining two separate environments momentarily, which the question states should be avoided.

Tip: Immutable deployments offer the safest and most automated way to roll out new versions without risking downtime or exposure to unhealthy releases, and do not require the overhead of a full duplicate environment like Blue/Green deployments.

Correct Answers:

  • Use the AWS CloudFormation Validate Template operation to confirm the template's code is correct. The Validate Template API checks that your CloudFormation file is correctly structured JSON or YAML.   • Run the AWS CloudFormation Validate Template command to ensure the properties of resources in the template are valid. The best choice is Implement a standby deployment in a secondary AWS region and use Route 53 failover routing to direct users to the standby in the event the main site becomes unavailable. This is known as a warm standby or active/passive DR pattern, which allows for quick failover with pre-provisioned resources, meeting a 1-hour RTO requirement for the entire multi-tier application. A warm standby allows for faster recovery compared to re-deployment or recreating from snapshots, since resources are already running and only need to be promoted or pointed to through DNS failover.

Looking at the other options:

Set up frequent EBS snapshots using EBS Lifecycle Manager to capture your volumes each hour focuses on protecting EBS volumes but does not address recovery of the whole stack, nor does it ensure the rapid recovery of application and database layers as required in a cross-region scenario.

Configure your RDS instances to take automated hourly snapshots and replicate them to another region increases database durability, but this technique alone does not guarantee the availability of compute and frontend resources in another region, and restoration from snapshots can take longer than desired for a strict RTO.

Create a Jenkins automation that generates AMIs for your EC2 servers every hour and triggers them through a scheduled pipeline provides automated server image creation, but it does not solve rapid, full application recovery by itself—re-deploying everything from AMIs can be slower than failing over to a warm standby.

Tip: For strict RTOs, a DR setup that maintains running resources in a failover region (warm standby or even active-active) is the most effective way to ensure your application can be restored within the required window.

This scenario illustrates both a Blue/Green deployment and a Red/Black deployment. Blue/Green deployment is a pattern where two identical environments are used; one runs the live version ('blue') while the new version is rolled out onto the idle environment ('green'). After testing, traffic is switched to the new environment. The same approach is often called Red/Black deployment (the terms are interchangeable, though Blue/Green is more common in AWS).

The answer is not A/B testing as that approach involves diverting traffic between multiple application versions simultaneously to gather data or run experiments, which is not the case here. Rolling deployment refers to gradually updating instances within the same environment without using separate groups—here, the deployment is performed completely on the secondary ASG. Canary deployment involves releasing a new version to a small subset of users before a complete cutover, rather than switching all traffic at once.

Tips: In the AWS context, Blue/Green and Red/Black both describe swapping between entire environments with zero overlap in user traffic; it guarantees easy rollback and minimal risk.

With Auto Scaling Lifecycle hooks, it's crucial to manage the timing so that you can complete all necessary customizations:

  • By using heartbeats, you can extend the Lifecycle hook's waiting period. This is essential if your configuration sometimes takes longer than anticipated, letting your process continue without being forced to move to the next Lifecycle hook action too early.

Set up the Lifecycle hook to restart its time period as soon as the software installation is complete doesn't make sense, as you should move the instance forward when configuration is done – there's no value in starting the waiting period over at that point.

The best deployment method in this scenario is the Immutable deployment strategy. With this approach, Elastic Beanstalk launches a completely new batch of instances using the new application version, independently of the old ones. Only after these new instances pass their health checks does traffic get directed to them. This method ensures zero-downtime deployments, and in case of failures, makes it easy to revert without impacting the original instances. Additionally, you maintain just one environment and do not need to run two parallel environments at all times.

Why are the other options incorrect?

  • Use a Rolling upgrade to deploy each version gradually to batches in the existing environment, attaching updated instances to the load balancer as they become healthy. – Although Rolling deployments reduce downtime by updating a few instances at a time, there is still a period where both new and old versions are running, which may cause some instability or partial outages if a batch fails. Also, failed health checks can cause a rollback to take longer and potentially impact some users.
  • Select a Rolling with extra batch option that launches an extra set of instances during each deployment for safer and more controlled updates. – While adding an extra batch reduces the likelihood of full-scale downtime, it does not fully isolate the new version from the old like Immutable deployments do. Partial updates still occur in the existing environment, and a faulty deployment could impact some users.
  • Adopt a blue/green deployment by setting up two separate environments and swapping URLs once the new version is verified. – Blue/green deployments fulfill the requirement of only serving traffic after new instances pass health checks, but they require running two environments concurrently, which was explicitly stated as not desired in the scenario.

Tip: Choose Immutable deployments in Elastic Beanstalk when you want zero-downtime updates with the highest level of reliability, health check integration, and simple rollback capability—without the hassle of maintaining two complete environments.

The correct answer is: The scheduled scaling process will start at 8:45 AM because the cooldown resets when a new scaling activity begins, and scheduled scaling waits for the cooldown to finish.

Here’s why: When a scaling event occurs in an Auto Scaling Group, such as responding to a CloudWatch alarm at 7:45 AM, the cooldown timer starts. Any other scaling activities—including scheduled actions—will only execute after the cooldown timer has expired. In this scenario, since the cooldown is set for 45 minutes, the next scaling activity (the scheduled action set for 8:00 AM) must wait until the cooldown completes, which will be at 8:45 AM. Scheduled actions do not override cooldowns; they must wait for the cooldown period to finish.

Let's examine why the other options are incorrect:

  • The scaling action scheduled for 8:00 AM will not run at all due to the active cooldown period, but will be available the next day. – This isn’t accurate. The scheduled action isn’t skipped; it’s simply delayed and will execute as soon as the cooldown is over.
  • The scheduled scaling operation kicks off immediately at 8:00 AM, as scheduled scaling actions are not restricted by the cooldown setting. – This is a misconception. Scheduled scaling actions are indeed subject to cooldown periods, so this is incorrect.
  • The scheduled scaling will commence at 8:30 AM, after the cooldown expires. – Since the cooldown began at 7:45 AM and is set for 45 minutes, it will end at 8:30 AM, so the scheduled scaling will actually occur at 8:45 AM, not 8:30 AM.

Tip: Always keep in mind that cooldown periods apply to both simple scaling activities and scheduled actions, delaying further scaling processes until the cooldown ends.

The correct answer is: Alter Stack Beta to eliminate the cross-stack import so it no longer imports the output from Stack Alpha.

Here's why:

  • As long as a resource output is being imported by another stack, you cannot remove or modify that export from the exporting stack (Stack Alpha). Therefore, you cannot delete Stack Alpha (Delete Stack Alpha via the AWS Console...), nor can you remove or change the resource output in Stack Alpha (Edit Stack Alpha to delete the output... and Modify Stack Alpha to update the exported security group's name in its output value.) while Stack Beta still references that value.

  • To safely make changes to the export or delete Stack Alpha, you must first update Stack Beta so that it no longer imports the value. This breaks the dependency, freeing Stack Alpha for changes. Thus, updating Stack Beta to remove the cross-stack reference is the only viable action here.

Tips:
  • When using CloudFormation cross-stack references, always remove the imports before making changes or deletions to the exports.
  • If you attempt to delete or modify an exported value that is being imported elsewhere, CloudFormation will block the operation and show a dependency error.

Summary: Remove cross-stack references first from importing stacks before changing or deleting outputs in exporting stacks.

The recommended solution is to deploy the new application component as an Elastic Beanstalk application, collect replies via the APIs, store the records in DynamoDB, and use Apache Hive with Amazon EMR for analytics. This design offers the following key advantages:

  • Durability and Accessibility: DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database with high durability and immediate accessibility, ideal for real-time and historical data storage for analytics.
  • Scalable Analytics: Amazon EMR and Apache Hive can efficiently analyze vast amounts of structured and semi-structured data at any time, leveraging the data stored in DynamoDB.
  • Seamless Integration: Elastic Beanstalk simplifies deployment and scaling for your Ruby application, while DynamoDB and EMR integrate naturally with other AWS analytics tools.

Why the other options are unsuitable:

  • "Set up the new component in an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to retrieve the social replies, save the data on Amazon EBS volumes, and utilize AWS Data Pipeline to send it to Amazon Kinesis for analysis."
    Amazon EBS volumes are attached to specific EC2 instances and are not inherently durable or accessible outside those instances. Storing analytics data on EBS is not recommended for long-term, highly available, or scalable analytics workflows.
  • "Deploy the new component as an Amazon Elastic Beanstalk application, retrieve replies from the social network, store replies on Amazon EBS, and stream the results into Amazon CloudWatch for analysis using Amazon Kinesis."
    This process uses EBS again (which is not recommended for long-term storage), and Amazon CloudWatch is primarily designed for metrics and logs, not large-scale historical data analytics.
  • "Launch the new component on an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances, extract replies from social media, archive the data in Amazon Glacier, and use AWS Data Pipeline to transmit it to Amazon Redshift for analytical purposes."
    Amazon Glacier is designed for cold/archival storage, making it unsuitable for applications requiring frequent and low-latency access to recent and historical analytics data.

Tips & Insights: Always pair highly durable, low-latency data stores (like DynamoDB, S3, or Redshift) with analytics tools for business intelligence use cases—avoid EBS and Glacier for such data. Use managed services like Elastic Beanstalk for simplified deployments and scaling.

To troubleshoot a failed AWS CloudFormation stack creation when rollback is disabled, the most effective methods are:

  • Inspect the event history of your CloudFormation stack using the AWS CloudFormation console. The console provides a live timeline of events, status changes, and error messages associated with individual resources in your stack, enabling you to quickly identify which resources failed and why.
  • Examine the instance logs located in /var/log/ on Amazon EC2, focusing on cfn and cloud-init logs, if your problem is related to EC2 resources. If the failure involves Amazon EC2 instances (such as bootstrapping or configuration issues), reviewing the /var/log/cloud-init.log and /var/log/cfn-init.log files on the affected instance can provide detailed steps of what was executed and pinpoint misconfigurations or errors.

The option Leverage AWS Config to trace every API call initiated by your CloudFormation stack is incorrect because AWS Config is designed for configuration tracking and compliance, not real-time debugging of API calls or stack events. Similarly, Enable CloudTrail to track and debug all API operations performed by the CloudFormation stack is not the most practical answer in this scenario. While CloudTrail does record API calls for auditing and security, it lacks context about CloudFormation resource life-cycles and failure reasons; it is not a troubleshooting tool for stack creation issues. For rapid and detailed debugging, rely on the CloudFormation console and resource-specific logs.

Tip: Always utilize the CloudFormation console's Events tab first for high-level troubleshooting, and if your stack provisions EC2 resources, collect logs from the instances for further diagnosis.

Tip: Use an integration response mapping template when you need to modify or filter the response payload from the backend before it is returned to the client—especially when managing API version compatibility.

The most reliable and direct way to ensure your SQL update script runs exactly once with each deployment in Elastic Beanstalk is by using a 'Solo Command' in your configuration files. The Elastic Beanstalk service coordinates the execution environment so the Solo Command is executed a single time on only one instance, effectively avoiding race conditions or duplicate migrations.

Choosing 'Leverage an EC2 metadata check to see if the instance is the leader...' is not an accurate or natively supported method in Elastic Beanstalk deployments; there is no built-in Auto Scaling group leader concept for reliable scripting in this context.

Modifying the database security groups as stated in 'Adjust the RDS security group to permit write access solely from one EC2 instance...' is an insecure and administratively challenging workaround, introducing possible points of failure and single-instance dependence. It is not advisable for production or automated deployments.

'Include a Container command with the leader only setting enabled...' is close—in Elastic Beanstalk, container commands with 'leader_only: true' can be used, but Solo Command is specifically designed for this use-case and is the best-practice approach preferred by AWS for idempotent, singleton operations during a deployment.

  • Tip: Use Solo Commands for tasks requiring only one execution regardless of the fleet size during Elastic Beanstalk deployments.
  • Do not rely on EC2-level metadata lookups for coordination in this scenario.
  • Security group changes as a singleton enforcement tool are not scalable or reliable.

The recommended strategies to avoid DynamoDB throttling when demand is uncertain are to Monitor the ConsumedReadCapacityUnits and ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits metrics in CloudWatch and Set up a CloudWatch alarm that triggers an AWS Lambda function to adjust the Read and Write throughput of your DynamoDB table.

First, tracking consumption metrics allows you to recognize when your application's traffic is nearing the allotted capacity, giving you valuable early warnings. This proactive approach helps you spot potential performance issues before they impact your users.

Second, connecting a CloudWatch alarm to a Lambda function can automate scaling operations. When thresholds are breached, Lambda can increase your table's capacity, helping avoid any throttling events resulting from surges in application requests.

The other choices are not ideal: Use CloudWatch to track the SystemErrors metric for DynamoDB is not as effective because SystemErrors don't necessarily reflect throttling situations—they indicate internal server errors, not traffic-induced constraints. Meanwhile, Configure a CloudWatch alarm that activates AWS Lambda to launch an entirely new DynamoDB table is not a scalable or practical solution, as it doesn't solve throttling and introduces operational overhead. Replicating tables isn't usually an answer to fluctuating capacity needs.

Tip: Always monitor actual usage versus provisioned capacity, and leverage automation with Lambda to adjust capacity in response to real-time traffic.

The best approach is to declare the parameter in the user parameters of the CodePipeline stage and then retrieve it from the event object passed to the Lambda function. When CodePipeline invokes a Lambda function as an action in a stage, it passes a JSON event. Any user parameters set on the action are included in the event['CodePipeline.job']['data']['actionConfiguration']['configuration']['UserParameters'] field within this JSON. This allows you to efficiently and securely pass values, such as a URL, from your pipeline definition directly to the Lambda execution environment for each invocation.

The option "Use an API Gateway endpoint that CodePipeline triggers, passing the parameter as a querystring to the Lambda function behind the API Gateway" adds unnecessary complexity, introducing another service (API Gateway) just for parameter passing, and is less secure and efficient than direct event transmission.

"Initiate a CloudFormation stack within the Lambda function, using the CodePipeline parameter with the “!Ref” intrinsic function for value resolution" is incorrect because CloudFormation is meant for infrastructure as code, not for transient parameter passing in runtime workloads like Lambda function invocations within pipelines.

"Specify the value as an environment variable in the new CodePipeline stage and access it in Lambda, for example in Python using os.environ["Parameter_Name"]." is also incorrect. Lambda environment variables are set at deployment time, not dynamically per pipeline execution, so you can't use this method to pass different values each run directly from a CodePipeline stage.

Tip: Always prefer using CodePipeline's user-defined parameters for passing context-specific values to Lambda actions, as this method is secure, auditable, and integrates natively with AWS services.

Amazon ElastiCache and Amazon RDS Read Replicas are the best choices for scaling the data tier and reducing query load for a read-intensive application:

  • Add Amazon ElastiCache: Caching common queries in ElastiCache (either Redis or Memcached) means subsequent requests can be served from in-memory storage, greatly reducing the number of queries that hit the RDS database and improving response times. This is particularly effective for data that doesn't change frequently or is requested often.
  • Introduce an Amazon RDS Read Replica: Read replicas let you offload read-heavy workloads from the primary DB instance to one or more replicas, which can be used to service read-only queries, thereby alleviating bottlenecks on the main RDS instance.

Why the other options are less suitable:

  • Set up Auto Scaling for your database tier to automatically add and remove database servers based on demand. – Traditional Auto Scaling is not natively supported for RDS databases since RDS instances do not scale horizontally in the same way EC2 instances do. Scaling up an RDS instance usually requires changing the instance type or adding read replicas, not Auto Scaling groups.
  • Utilize SQS to store query results for quick access. – Amazon SQS is designed for reliable message queuing between components of distributed systems. It's not a caching mechanism and isn't designed for storing or retrieving query results, so it would not help reduce direct database read loads.

Tip: For read-intensive applications, effective caching and the use of read replicas are AWS best practices to drastically improve performance and scalability at the database layer.

Tip: Always ensure that no other stacks are consuming exported values before making changes to exports or deleting stacks. This ensures safe and successful operations in multi-stack CloudFormation environments.

The correct answer is: It is not possible to change a Security Group's name within a .ebextensions config file. Adjust the eb config script to utilize the desired Security Group.

This is because .ebextensions is mainly intended to manage environment resources and settings not already governed by the environment's core configuration, such as through EB CLI commands or the AWS Management Console. Specifically, network-level components like Security Groups, which are implemented at the environment level, are not modifiable post-creation through .ebextensions. These settings must be handled by updating the configuration via the EB CLI (eb config) or directly through AWS.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • There is a precedence issue: the .ebextensions config was handled prior to the eb config command in the deployment process, so the eb config value overwrote it. Update the Jenkins job so that the .ebextensions config runs after executing eb config. – The order of processing does not allow .ebextensions to supersede EB CLI-set values for Security Groups. The fundamental limitation is with what .ebextensions can control.
  • Conflicting values between .ebextensions and eb config cause Elastic Beanstalk to default to the built-in option. The solution is to remove the Security Group assignment from eb config to avoid ambiguity. – In practice, Elastic Beanstalk does not simply fall back to a default if there is a conflict; the Security Group set through the EB CLI takes priority.
  • The .ebextensions directory settings are not able to override those configured through the EB CLI. To resolve this, eliminate the Security Group configuration from the eb config command. – While this is somewhat correct, it's more accurate to update the EB CLI (or the environment configuration) to use the correct Security Group since .ebextensions cannot perform this function.

Tip: For network or environment-level configurations, always use the AWS Console or the EB CLI rather than .ebextensions. Reserve .ebextensions for resource and software configuration tasks within your environment.
