Supported deployment configurations for Lambda in AWS CodeDeploy include CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery10Minutes, CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce, and CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes. These are the default strategies:

  • CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce: All incoming traffic is moved to the new Lambda version in a single step. This is the fastest method, but offers no safety net in case of issues.
  • CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery10Minutes: Gradually shifts 10% of traffic every 10 minutes until all traffic is using the new Lambda version. This reduces risk and allows rollback if issues are detected.
  • CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes: Sends 10% of traffic to the new version initially, and if no problems occur, shifts the remaining 90% after five minutes. This is an effective way to catch errors quickly before impacting everyone.

The options CodeDeployDefault.AllAtATime, CodeDeployDefault.LambdaHalf, and CodeDeployDefault.Immutable are not valid Lambda deployment configurations supported by AWS CodeDeploy. CodeDeployDefault.AllAtATime is not an actual supported configuration for Lambda, CodeDeployDefault.LambdaHalf does not exist, and CodeDeployDefault.Immutable relates to ECS/on-premise deployments, not Lambda. When deploying Lambda functions, choose among the officially supported strategies listed above to ensure smooth rollouts and reduce risk. Tip: Always review AWS CodeDeploy documentation for the latest supported configurations specific to Lambda to avoid confusion between resource types.

Set up a parallel Elastic Beanstalk environment and use the Swap Environment URLs feature is the preferred deployment method for minimizing downtime during application rollbacks. Implement Rolling Updates within Elastic Beanstalk, which will automatically revert to the previous version if any update fails is incorrect because while Rolling Updates can reduce downtime and offer basic rollback function if failures are detected, they do not guarantee a near-instant rollback for all types of potential failures—especially when issues only surface after deployment completes.

Develop an AWS CloudFormation template to duplicate your Beanstalk resources, and manually deploy this if needed to control rollbacks is not ideal for urgent rollback needs as creating and deploying resources via CloudFormation is typically slower, more manual, and subject to greater risk of configuration drift or error.

Tip: Using parallel environments with the Swap URL feature is a best practice for AWS Beanstalk zero-downtime deployments and reliable, fast rollback with critical workloads.

Establish a backup and restore process: schedule daily backups of Jenkins configuration files to Amazon S3, and use CloudFormation to quickly redeploy resources if necessary. is the most suitable option in this scenario.

  • Both RTO and RPO are set at 24 hours, which means your organization can tolerate up to 24 hours without the Jenkins server and up to 24 hours of data loss. The backup & restore pattern is the most cost-effective and operationally simple approach when recovery can be reasonably handled within these windows.
  • Automating regular backups of configuration files to S3 ensures that you always have a recent copy ready for restoration. Combining this with CloudFormation allows for automated and consistent re-provisioning of the server infrastructure, keeping recovery simple and within the permitted RTO/RPO.

The other options are less appropriate for these requirements:

  • Implement a Warm Standby solution: launch a smaller-scale EC2 server in another VPC within the same region to act as a standby Jenkins instance. — Warm standby strategies are designed for lower RTO/RPO; typically minutes to an hour. They are more costly because they keep servers running and ready, which isn’t necessary when 24-hour windows are acceptable.
  • Set up a Pilot Light configuration: maintain an AMI image so an EC2 instance can be launched in a different region and kept off to minimize costs, starting it when needed. — While pilot light is used for reduced cost, it is often more complex to implement than basic backup & restore, and is more suited when infrastructure and application state need to be preserved and restored rapidly.
  • Deploy a Hot Standby solution: provision a fully running EC2 server mirroring the Jenkins environment, but pause its workload unless a failover is triggered. — Hot standby (multi-site) solutions are intended for organizations that require minimal downtime and minimal-to-zero data loss (very low RTO/RPO). This is far beyond the requirements here and much more expensive to maintain.

Tip: Always align your disaster recovery solution to your actual RTO/RPO needs. When 24 hours is sufficient, simple daily backups and automated restoration can save both money and complexity.

The most appropriate solution is to use the deletion policy of type Snapshot on the Amazon RDS resource within the AWS CloudFormation template. This ensures that, when the CloudFormation stack is deleted, a DB snapshot of the database is automatically created, preserving all test data for future access and restoration as needed. This policy is tailored for temporary resources that hold valuable information needing retention after automated infrastructure teardown.

Option "Set up a dependency relationship using the DependsOn attribute between the master Amazon RDS instance and a read replica in the testing stack." is incorrect because the DependsOn attribute only manages the order of resource creation and does not affect the retention or deletion of resources after the stack is removed. It is not intended for data preservation.

Option "Designate an update policy that will prevent the Amazon RDS database from being deleted when the CloudFormation stack is removed." is not feasible. Update policies are used for controlling resource update behavior (mainly for Auto Scaling groups or similar) and do not influence deletion protection.

Option "Assign a deletion policy of type Retain to the RDS resource to ensure the RDS instance is preserved after CloudFormation deletes the stack." would leave the entire database running and available, which might incur unnecessary costs and is not typically aligned with the purpose of ephemeral test environments. Retaining the full instance is often unnecessary just for data preservation.

Option "Establish automated backups with a 30-day backup retention policy for Amazon RDS and plan to perform a point-in-time restoration if data access is necessary after stack removal." depends on scheduled backups, which may not capture all the test data—especially if testing is short lived. Backups also introduce complexities in restoring and accessing the data as needed since point-in-time recovery may not be practical in this use case.

Tip: Always evaluate whether you need the actual resource to persist or just need a backup or snapshot for compliance or data recovery. For temporary stacks with crucial data, the Snapshot deletion policy is optimal as it manages costs and ensures data protection.

The best options are Apply the UpdatePolicy attribute together with the AutoScalingRollingUpdate feature in CloudFormation to perform code deployments. and Define update policies on Auto Scaling groups within your CloudFormation template and then redeploy. Both approaches leverage CloudFormation's rolling update capabilities, which allow updates to occur incrementally across your Auto Scaling group instances. This method ensures that only a portion of instances are updated at any given time, thus minimizing downtime and helping control costs since you don't need to run two full sets of resources.

The other choices are less appropriate. Redeploy your application from scratch with a CloudFormation template for each update introduces unnecessary downtime and resource use, as it typically requires tearing down and re-creating resources rather than updating only what is necessary. As each CloudFormation stack finishes updating, immediately remove the previous stack can also lead to downtime and higher costs, because it assumes a full tear-down and setup process rather than an in-place rolling update, and managing state transitions between stacks can be complex.

Tips: Use CloudFormation UpdatePolicy with Auto Scaling groups to automate rolling updates. Always test update procedures in a lower environment to validate minimal disruption.

Tips: For fine-grained control and extensibility, always prefer event-driven architectures (CloudWatch Events/EventBridge + Lambda) for reacting to AWS infrastructure changes, as this pattern allows customization and integration with many notification and messaging platforms.

The correct entry for connecting to a specific CodeCommit regional endpoint is Host git-codecommit.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com User APKAXXXXXXXXXEXAMPLE IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa. This format matches the required hostname structure for CodeCommit in a given region, paired with the IAM SSH username (the SSH key ID) and the correct private key.

Let's examine why the others don't work:

  • Host * User IAMUSREIDEXAMPLE IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa: This would apply to all SSH connections but 'IAMUSREIDEXAMPLE' is not a valid CodeCommit IAM SSH username (which must match the SSH key ID).
  • Host git-codecommit.*.amazonaws.com User IAMUSREIDEXAMPLE IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub.: The wildcard host is not supported by CodeCommit and the identity file must be the private key (not the .pub public key). 'IAMUSREIDEXAMPLE' is also not accepted unless it matches the actual upload ID.
  • Host git-codecommit.*.amazonaws.com User APKAXXXXXXXXXEXAMPLE IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa: Again, CodeCommit does not accept wildcards for regional endpoints. You must specify the correct region per entry.

Tips: Always match the CodeCommit regional hostname and use the SSH username generated in IAM. Set IdentityFile to your private key. Wildcard hosts and incorrect usernames will result in authentication errors.

When the S3 service is impaired or unavailable, any attempt to launch a new EC2 instance from an EBS snapshot can fail because the underlying snapshot data cannot be accessed. This explains why your current EC2 instances (which do not require S3 to continue operating unless you are attaching a snapshot) are fine, but you are unable to start new ones from snapshots during the S3 outage.

Why the other answers are incorrect:

  • To prevent system overload, AWS disables all EC2 API calls during serious outages. — AWS does not disable all EC2 API calls as a blanket measure even during major outages. Existing running instances and some API operations may continue even under partial outages.

Tip: If you experience failures when restoring from EBS snapshots during AWS outages, always check the S3 service health dashboard, as snapshot restore and creation depend on S3's infrastructure. Understanding cross-service dependencies is key for troubleshooting AWS outages.

AWS CodePipeline is highly flexible and supports multiple third-party and AWS native integrations for each stage. These combinations reflect valid provider options in each stage:

  • Bitbucket/Jenkins/S3: CodePipeline supports Bitbucket as a source, Jenkins builds, and S3 as a deployment target for static asset pipelines.

You can integrate with third-party tools such as Jenkins or GitHub as source or build providers, while AWS CodeBuild serves as a default managed build service.   • AWS CloudTrail tracks API calls and account activity for auditing but does not offer native notification delivery mechanisms or direct event pattern matching needed for instant alerts.

  • CreationPolicy: This is used to indicate that AWS CloudFormation should wait for some condition (like a signal) before marking the resource as created. It does not affect how resources are handled during replacement.

Tip: Use UpdateReplacePolicy with values such as Retain, Snapshot, or Delete for finer control over resource lifecycle in update scenarios. Make sure to set it explicitly in your template when resource retention during replacement is required.

The correct step is to read every block on EBS volumes restored from snapshots to pre-warm them before running your tests. Amazon EBS volumes restored from snapshots are lazy-loaded, meaning that only data requested is loaded on first access, causing initial read operations to experience higher latency. By pre-warming (reading all blocks), you ensure that your I/O performance test measures the actual, steady-state performance of the volume, not the initial slowness caused by lazy loading.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Randomize the selection of I/O block sizes in each test run: This introduces variability, which makes your performance tests less repeatable. Consistency in test parameters is vital to obtain reliable results.
  • Back up EBS volumes by creating snapshots prior to each test: While snapshotting is useful for data backup, it does not impact the I/O performance characteristics of the volume during testing, nor does it resolve issues related to lazy loading.
  • Encrypt the underlying EBS volume before testing to ensure stability: Encryption does not guarantee consistent I/O performance, and it is not required for accurate performance benchmarking unless part of your workflow involves encrypted volumes specifically.

Tip: For accurate and repeatable I/O performance tests with EBS volumes, always ensure volumes are fully initialized and pre-warmed prior to running benchmarks, especially after restoring from a snapshot.

The correct answer is Apply UpdatePolicy: AutoScalingReplacingUpdate: WillReplace: true.

This UpdatePolicy tells CloudFormation to replace the entire Auto Scaling group during a stack update, meaning it will create a new group with the latest configuration and remove the old group in the cleanup phase. This is necessary when changes like a new launch template or different instance types require full replacement.

Let's examine why other options are not suitable:

  • Set UpdatePolicy: AutoScalingReplacingUpdate: WillReplace: false. – This option instructs CloudFormation not to replace the Auto Scaling group, but rather to update it in place, which does not address requirements where a group replacement is essential.
  • Configure UpdatePolicy: AutoScalingRollingUpdate with MinInstancesInService: 0 and WaitOnResourceSignals: true. – Rolling updates change instances within the group without replacing the group itself, so it won't create and remove an entirely new Auto Scaling group. This does not fit the scenario's criteria.
  • Use UpdatePolicy: AutoScalingScheduledAction: IgnoreUnmodifiedGroupSizeProperties: true. – ScheduledAction update policy is specific to scheduled scaling actions and unrelated to replacing or updating the Auto Scaling group during stack updates.

Tip: Use AutoScalingReplacingUpdate: WillReplace: true whenever you want CloudFormation to swap out an entire Auto Scaling group for a new one rather than just updating the existing group. Always test template changes in a non-production environment to confirm expected behavior.

Lambda@Edge functions can be triggered at four primary CloudFront lifecycle events: Viewer request, Origin request, Origin response, and Viewer response. These trigger points allow developers to execute code at the edge, enabling dynamic selection of A/B test content without changing the web application's core codebase.

Why the correct choices are right:

  • Viewer request: Occurs when CloudFront receives a request from an end user—ideal for handling content selection before the cache or origin is consulted.
  • Origin request: Triggered when CloudFront forwards a request to your origin (web server, etc.), useful when modifying headers or selecting content after cache miss.
  • Origin response: Initiated when CloudFront receives a response from the origin, which enables content modification right before it's cached or sent back to the user.
  • Viewer response: Happens just as CloudFront sends a response to the user, allowing final alterations or header manipulations before content delivery.

CloudFront cache is not a supported Lambda@Edge event. It does not represent a trigger point for Lambda execution; it's a storage mechanism where files are cached, but no code execution occurs directly at this phase.

Tip: To perform advanced content personalization or A/B testing at the edge, use Lambda@Edge at the appropriate event hook that matches the logic you wish to apply. Understanding where these hooks fit into the CloudFront request/response cycle is crucial for optimizing performance and capability.

Afterwards, you should invoke ContinueUpdateRollback with the ResourcesToSkip parameter, which allows CloudFormation to mark the skipped resources as UPDATE_COMPLETE and continue the rollback operation. If, during stack deletion, a DELETE_FAILED status is encountered, making use of DeleteStack along with the RetainResources parameter enables you to remove the stack while retaining non-removable resources.

Let's break down why the options are correct or incorrect:

  • Enable termination protection on the stack to prevent deletion. Next, initiate a ContinueUpdateRollback using the ResourcesToSkip parameter, allowing CloudFormation to mark listed resources as UPDATE_COMPLETE and proceed with the rollback.   • After the stack enters UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, make any required adjustments outside of CloudFormation to align with its expected state. Then, perform ContinueUpdateRollback and specify ResourcesToSkip for CloudFormation to push those resources to UPDATE_COMPLETE before proceeding with rollback. If a DELETE_FAILED status is encountered during deletion, use DeleteStack along with RetainResources to delete the stack, keeping those undeletable resources.: This option correctly outlines the recommended step-by-step remediation process, specifying both drift correction and use of stack actions for cleanup.

Stack protection alone does not contribute to resolving UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED states or resource drift.
  • Initiate UpdateTerminationProtection to guard against accidental deletions. Run ContinueUpdateRollback with ResourcesToSkip to advance the rollback. If a DELETE_FAILED state occurs while deleting, utilize DeleteStack and RetainResources to remove the stack but keep the affected resources.: While this acknowledges the use of ContinueUpdateRollback and RetainResources, it wrongly emphasizes termination protection and misorders the steps, potentially causing confusion.

Tip: The key to resolving stack drift and failed updates is using ContinueUpdateRollback with ResourcesToSkip, and, if deletion fails, leveraging DeleteStack with RetainResources. Ensure the stack resources are as expected before retrying rollback operations.

Implement an AWS Config rule to evaluate whether CloudFormation stack resources have drifted from their template definitions. If the rule detects NON_COMPLIANT status, notify the team using an SNS topic is the most suitable solution. AWS Config offers managed rules that can monitor configuration drift within CloudFormation stacks, allowing for automatic compliance checking and integrated notification. This enables proactive and automated detection and alerting without needing custom scripts or polling logic.

Let’s review why the other alternatives are not ideal:

Configure a Lambda function to periodically check each CloudFormation stack for configuration drift every ten minutes, and if drift is detected, use AWS SES to notify the team by email. – While this could work, it requires building and managing a custom Lambda function and scheduler, which is more complex and less reliable than native drift detection features.

Set up a CloudWatch Events rule to monitor all CloudFormation stack events, and use SNS to trigger an email alert for any event related to CloudFormation. – CloudWatch Events do not specifically filter drift events, so this would generate unnecessary alerts for routine stack activity, making it difficult to distinguish actual drift cases.

Activate CloudTrail and use a Lambda function to parse CloudTrail logs, sending an email whenever stack resources are found to have been changed outside of CloudFormation. – Parsing CloudTrail logs for drift detection is cumbersome, not real-time, and could miss relevant changes. It also requires considerable custom development.

Tip: Using AWS Config managed rules makes drift detection simpler and builds in automated notification and compliance tracking.

Both methods enable proper authentication using the on-premises LDAP and leverage AWS IAM Security Token Service (STS) to obtain temporary credentials, promoting secure, scalable, and standards-aligned access.

  • Switch the deployment method from Rolling to All at Once. – Changing the deployment type does not address the underlying issue of health check failures; even in an all-at-once deployment, failed health checks can cause rollback.

Tip: Use the 'Ignore health check' option only when you are certain the health check issue is understood and not unexpected, as ignoring legitimate health failures can allow faulty code into production.

The correct answer is: Leverage roles that permit federated web identity users to assume a role, granting temporary credentials that allow access to the Redshift table.

This method uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles in combination with web identity federation (e.g., Amazon Cognito, Facebook, Google, or other supported identity providers). The application can request temporary, limited-privilege credentials. This approach reduces the risk associated with long-term credentials, supports best security practices (like least privilege and credential rotation), and is tailor-made for mobile and web applications where user access is dynamic and needs tight security controls.

Let's discuss why the others are incorrect:

  • Set up an HSM client certificate for Redshift and use this certificate for authentication. - Redshift does not support external client certificates for authentication via Hardware Security Modules (HSMs). This option does not correctly address Redshift's security model and is not viable.
  • Create a Redshift read-only policy in IAM and include the static credentials in the application code. - Embedding long-term IAM credentials within application code is a significant security vulnerability. If the application is ever decompiled or exposed, these credentials could be stolen, leading to unauthorized access and potential data breaches.
  • Provision an IAM user, generate encryption keys, and configure a policy for read-only Redshift access. Embed these keys within the app. - Similar to the previous option, embedding encryption keys or access credentials within the application poses a high security risk. Keys can be extracted and misused, and managing rotation and revocation becomes very challenging.

Tip: Always use temporary credentials and identity federation when building mobile or web apps that interact with AWS, to avoid hard-coding credentials and improve overall security.

The most effective solution is to Integrate an Amazon SQS queue between your web layer and DynamoDB to help buffer heavy bursts of requests during peak times. By leveraging SQS, your application can decouple the influx of requests from direct interaction with DynamoDB, smoothing out spikes during times like the 9:00AM user rush. This helps prevent the DynamoDB table's provisioned capacity from being overwhelmed, thereby minimizing throttling and improving user experience.

The option Switch your Auto Scaling group to use Amazon C3 instances to address potential compute bottlenecks at the application layer is unrelated because the bottleneck resides in the database backend, not the levels of compute capacity.

While Move to an ElastiCache Memcached cluster in one Availability Zone to cache frequently accessed data in front of the web tier can help for cacheable data, depending solely on a single AZ risks availability, and caching alone doesn’t solve all DynamoDB throughput and partitioning issues.

Simply Increase the Write Capacity Units of your DynamoDB table, as write throttling may occur when users access the site may not be cost-effective, especially if the traffic spike is temporary; you could still have hot partitions, so it’s not the most efficient first step.

Lastly, Migrate the data to a new DynamoDB table with a more evenly distributed partition key, and adjust your application accordingly is a considerable architecture change—while it's best practice to design a good distribution up front, it's complex to execute just to solve sporadic traffic spikes.

  • Tip: For web applications experiencing short, predictable bursts of traffic, message queues like SQS can buffer and smooth workload to backend systems without the need for immediate and substantial scaling changes.

The correct solution is to Attach a CreationPolicy to the EC2 instance resource in your CloudFormation template. A CreationPolicy instructs CloudFormation to wait for a success signal (typically via cfn-signal) before marking the EC2 instance (and thus the stack) as successfully created. This ensures Apache and other software are fully set up and running before CloudFormation reports that the resource creation is complete.

Option Leverage lifecycle hooks so the stack marks completion only when all underlying resources are finished provisioning is incorrect because lifecycle hooks are a feature of Auto Scaling Groups, not regular CloudFormation stacks or individual resources.

Set a stack policy requiring all component resources to be active before the stack reflects a CREATE_COMPLETE status is not correct, as stack policies only control which resources can be updated or deleted, not how resources signal readiness.

Utilize CloudFormation helper scripts (such as cfn-signal) to inform CloudFormation once the configuration is done is an important part of the process but is incomplete by itself. Without a CreationPolicy attached, CloudFormation won't wait for the signal. You need both the CreationPolicy and use of cfn-signal for it to work as expected.

Tip: Always use CreationPolicy with resources that need extra configuration time—especially when bootstrapping servers—so CloudFormation only marks the stack as complete once all initialization scripts finish and software is running as desired.

The correct method in this scenario is to build a Docker container for your application and deploy it via Elastic Beanstalk. Elastic Beanstalk allows you to run applications inside Docker containers, making it possible to use any underlying platform or runtime, even if it's not offered natively by Beanstalk. This approach provides the flexibility to package your custom dependencies and run virtually any stack.

Let's review why the other options are not suitable:

  • Leverage AWS OpsWorks to generate a stack. Within the stack, establish a new custom layer, deploy your app there, and connect it to Elastic Beanstalk. – OpsWorks and Elastic Beanstalk are separate services, and there is no direct integration or benefit to connecting custom layers from OpsWorks to Beanstalk for deployment.
  • Craft custom CloudFormation templates to deploy the app directly into Elastic Beanstalk. – While CloudFormation can provision Elastic Beanstalk environments, it cannot inject a new platform. You still need to provide a supported application environment, so it doesn't resolve the problem of a missing platform.
  • Utilize specialized Chef recipes to install and run your app on Elastic Beanstalk. – Chef recipes and configuration can modify the environment, but you cannot fully customize the underlying platform with just Chef scripts inside Beanstalk. Docker containers provide much more control for unsupported stacks.

Tip: When your application's platform is not supported by AWS Elastic Beanstalk, containerization (especially Docker) is the most flexible and portable solution. This lets you leverage Beanstalk's deployment, scaling, and management features regardless of native platform support.

Assign all users full administrator access, allowing them to clone or push to all current and future CodeCommit repositories without restrictions is incorrect and considered a security risk. By aligning the PauseTime and CoolDown intervals with the real warm-up time, you prevent new instances from being considered unhealthy (and thus replaced prematurely) or excessive scaling from occurring.

Disable the SYN/ACK mechanism in TCP or switch to the UDP protocol is not a viable solution, as disabling TCP's handshake would break reliable connections, and switching protocols does not guarantee better throughput or reliability for most cluster compute workloads.

Write events to an SNS topic, subscribe each SQS queue, and use a Lambda function in each pipeline to poll and filter events from its queue is less efficient. Each SQS queue would receive all events, even the irrelevant ones, leading to unnecessary message processing and potential cost/waste.

Deliver events directly to an SQS queue, have a Lambda function extract, filter, and forward events to multiple SQS queues as needed introduces additional Lambda invocation and forwarding complexity, increasing latency, cost, and operational burden. It doesn't leverage AWS-native filtering available through SNS.

Use EventBridge as the event bus, have a Lambda pull, filter, and distribute messages to different SQS queues in parallel is more complex and typically unnecessary for straightforward fan-out and filtering to SQS queues. EventBridge is great for complex routing patterns, but SNS with subscription filters is simpler and better suited to this scenario.

Tip: Use SNS subscription filter policies to route messages efficiently to only those SQS queues that need them—no Lambda code required.

The correct approach is to define outputs in the network stack and export resources, then use the Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function in the application stack to import them. This mechanism allows you to share resources securely and efficiently between CloudFormation stacks while maintaining stack independence and decoupled management.

Here's why other options are not suitable:
- Export resources within the network stack's resource properties, and in the application stack, use the Fn::GetAtt intrinsic function to obtain them: Fn::GetAtt only works within the same stack or with nested stacks, not for cross-stack references through separate stacks.
- Export network stack outputs, then import those resources within the application stack by leveraging the Fn::Sub intrinsic function: Fn::Sub substitutes variables and doesn't retrieve values from exports; it can't perform stack-to-stack imports.
- Utilize Fn::ExportValue in the network stack to export resources, then apply Fn::FindInMap in the application stack to retrieve them: Fn::FindInMap is designed for mapping static values and cannot fetch outputs exported from another stack.

Tip: Exporting stack outputs and importing with Fn::ImportValue is the best-practice method for allowing loosely coupled CloudFormation stacks to reference shared resources like VPC subnets and security groups without directly linking the stacks.

The deploy a secondary Elastic Beanstalk environment with the new version, then swap the CNAMEs of the two environments approach (commonly known as Blue/Green Deployment) meets the requirements of zero downtime and rapid rollback. When you swap CNAMEs, DNS routing instantly switches all incoming traffic to the new version without interrupting service. If any issues are detected, a rollback is as easy as swapping the CNAMEs again—restoring the previous functioning environment nearly instantly.

The option to enable rolling deployment updates in your Elastic Beanstalk environment and set a suitable pause interval to account for application startup may help reduce downtime, but it doesn't offer near-instantaneous rollback and can sometimes result in brief service interruptions if a batch fails. The option to update your application so that it regularly checks for new code in the repository and applies updates independently on each instance is not a standard Elastic Beanstalk practice and is complicated to manage. It also does not provide proper rollback mechanisms. The suggestion to launch another Elastic Beanstalk environment with the updated version and set up a redirect (HTTP 301) in the old environment to send clients to the new one is not appropriate here—HTTP 301 redirects are permanent and can cause caching problems for clients, besides not providing a quick rollback mechanism.

Tip: Elastic Beanstalk's Blue/Green deployment model is specifically designed for scenarios that demand continuous delivery and rapid rollback in production environments. Familiarity with this deployment pattern is essential for AWS Solution Architect exams.

The best choice is to make the game identifier the partition key and HighestScore the sort key. This design ensures that scores are distributed based on the game, allowing queries for the top scores to be efficient and scalable. By using the game as the partition key, you distribute requests evenly across the partition space, which is essential for high-traffic scenarios and prevents "hot partitions." The HighestScore as the sort key then enables queries that quickly fetch the highest score for each game (by sorting in descending order and retrieving the first item).

The other options are suboptimal:

  • Use the UserID field as only the partition key. - This would spread data based on users, not games, making it hard to efficiently query for top scores per game.
  • Set UserID as the partition key and HighestScore as the sort key. - This pattern would partition data by users, not by game, causing similar inefficiencies for game-specific queries.
  • Choose the HighestScore column as the partition key. - Partitioning by score would cluster scores rather than spreading requests, leading to poor distribution, and you might face uneven workload and scaling issues.

Tip: Always align your DynamoDB key structure with your main access patterns, and choose partition keys that will result in balanced and scalable workloads.

The correct solution is to set the DeletionPolicy attribute to "Retain" in your CloudFormation template for the AWS::RDS::DBInstance resource. Let’s look at why the other choices are not suitable:

  • Configure a Read Replica in the RDS setup to ensure the replica remains available after deleting the stack. – Read Replicas are useful for scaling and high availability, but they do not protect your original DB instance upon stack deletion. Also, CloudFormation will remove replicas created within the template when the stack is deleted unless explicitly told to retain them.
  • Include a WaitPolicy property with the value "Retain" for the AWS::RDS::DBInstance resource in your CloudFormation template. – There is no WaitPolicy property in CloudFormation for RDS resources; thus, this option would not work or provide the desired behavior.
  • Change the DBInstanceClass property of the AWS::RDS::DBInstance to a read-only type in the template. – The DBInstanceClass property determines the instance size/type, not its data retention policy. It doesn't affect what happens when a stack is deleted and will not preserve your database.

Tip: Use the DeletionPolicy "Retain" on resources you want to keep after deleting a stack, especially for databases and persistent storage!

The correct answer is Configure an S3 Cross-Region Replication policy on the CloudTrail log bucket to copy logs to another bucket located in a different region.

Explanation:
Cross-Region Replication (CRR) for Amazon S3 buckets ensures the automatic and continuous copying of CloudTrail logs from their source bucket in one region to a target bucket in another region. This provides redundancy and disaster recovery capabilities: even if an entire region fails, critical audit trails and security information remain accessible in a separate region, protecting the organization from data loss.

Here's why the other options are not appropriate:

  • Turn on SSE-KMS encryption for the S3 bucket holding CloudTrail logs. — While encryption is important for securing data at rest, enabling SSE-KMS does NOT address regional outages or improve availability in the event of a disaster affecting the entire region.
  • Add a new S3 bucket in another AWS region directly from the CloudTrail console as an additional destination for the trail. — CloudTrail trails can only be configured with one destination S3 bucket per trail; you cannot specify multiple buckets (especially in different regions) directly from the console. This is a common misconception.
  • Deploy an AWS Lambda function that reads log files from the trail S3 bucket and manually copies the logs to another bucket in a different AWS region. — Although technically possible, this is a much more complex, less reliable, and less automated approach compared to simply using S3's built-in cross-region replication feature.

Tip: Use S3 Cross-Region Replication for critical log and audit data to enhance durability and compliance, especially when regional disasters or AWS region outages are a concern.
query: You have been hired as an AWS consultant for a growing tech startup. The company wants better insight into who is doing what within their AWS environment, so AWS CloudTrail has been enabled. Since most resources are located in the ap-south-1 region, CloudTrail has only been configured to track activity in this region, and logs are being sent to an Amazon S3 bucket located in ap-south-1. The client is now concerned about potential data loss if a disaster strikes the ap-south-1 AWS region. What can you do to ensure CloudTrail logs remain available even if the ap-south-1 region experiences a major outage or becomes unavailable?

options.text: Configure an S3 Cross-Region Replication policy on the CloudTrail log bucket to copy logs to another bucket located in a different region.
Turn on SSE-KMS encryption for the S3 bucket holding CloudTrail logs.
Add a new S3 bucket in another AWS region directly from the CloudTrail console as an additional destination for the trail.
Deploy an AWS Lambda function that reads log files from the trail S3 bucket and manually copies the logs to another bucket in a different AWS region.

originalQuery:
You are an AWS consultant working in a startup IT company.
The company wanted to increase visibility into its user and resource activity in AWS.
So CloudTrail was turned on.
As most resources were used in region ap-south-1, the trail was only configured to collect the activities in that region.
The CloudTrail is saved in an S3 bucket.
However, the customer is worried that if some disaster in region ap-south-1 happens, the CloudTrail data may get lost.
Which actions should you take to address the concern?
originalOptions: A. Enable the encryption with SSE-KMS for the S3 bucket of the CloudTrail.
B. In the CloudTrail console, add another S3 bucket in a different region as the target for the trail.
C. Enable Cross-Region Replication for the trail S3 bucket to automatically copy objects in a different AWS Region.
D. Create a Lambda Function that can read files in the trail S3 bucket and copy the log files to an S3 bucket in another region.
